slides.title: The money left, but never arrived
slides.tldr: If the two steps of one job are saved separately, a single error in between makes the money vanish.

blocks.body: Ryan sends $50 to Kevin from a wallet app. The code does two things: lower Ryan's balance, raise Kevin's. Each service method calls `flush()` internally, so each step is committed to the database on its own. If an exception hits after the first step, Ryan has been charged and Kevin has received nothing.

marks.tip: The moment this line finishes, the first change is permanent in the database. Whatever happens next, it will not undo itself.
Kevin's wallet is closed, the id is wrong, or a deploy lands right now: whatever stops this line from running, $50 disappears.

blocks.caption: An error between the two steps: who is left holding what

actors.label: Ryan
actors.tip: Wants to send Kevin $50. His balance was $100.

actors.label: Symfony app
actors.tip: Works in two steps: withdraw() first, deposit() second, each with its own flush().

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Commits every flush() as a separate transaction. It has no idea that the two steps belong to the same job.

messages.label: Ryan's balance $100 → $50
messages.tip: The flush() inside withdraw(). This change is committed immediately.
deposit() never runs. Once PHP has stopped, nobody is left to undo the earlier commit.

messages.label: 500 error
messages.tip: Ryan sees "failed", yet his money has already been taken.
The system as a whole has lost $50. This half-done state is exactly what a transaction prevents.

aside.title: "Money deducted, recipient got nothing"
aside.body: A wallet app kept getting two or three complaints a month: money deducted, recipient never received it. Testing alone never reproduced it. In the end the team found that a timeout or a deploy sometimes hit between the two steps, and each time the first half stayed in the database.

items.meaning: Running several changes as one indivisible unit of work.
Making all the changes of a transaction permanent.
Throwing away all the changes of a transaction and returning to the earlier state.

check.q: If the server dies between the two steps, what happens to Ryan's and Kevin's balances in this code?
check.a: Ryan's $50 stays deducted, because the first flush() was already committed. Kevin's balance doesn't change, so $50 vanishes from the total.

slides.title: ACID: the four promises of a transaction
slides.tldr: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: all or nothing, rules stay intact, half-done work stays hidden, committed means committed.

blocks.title: Sending money on Venmo
blocks.body: When you tap Send Money in a payment app like Venmo, you see one of two outcomes: "success" or "failed". You never see "your money left, but it didn't arrive". A database transaction gives you exactly that guarantee. Split the guarantee into four parts and you get ACID.

blocks.caption: The four letters of ACID, explained with a wallet transfer

cells: Every step happens, or none does
Debit and delivery both happen, or neither
rows.tip: If an error strikes midway, the database undoes the earlier steps itself (rollback). A half-done state is never left behind.

cells: A state that breaks the rules is never saved
A balance never drops below zero
rows.tip: The database only guards the rules you have written down as constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign keys, CHECK. Every other rule is your code's job.

cells: Other people's half-done work stays invisible
Someone looking midway still sees the old balance
rows.tip: The isolation level decides how separate concurrent transactions stay. The default level does not prevent every kind of mix-up.

cells: Once committed, it is never lost
Even if the power fails after "success", the money is there
rows.tip: Before answering the commit, the database writes the change to a log on disk (the WAL), so after a crash it can bring the change back.

marks.tip: Without this line a buggy debit would commit a balance of -100 and nothing would stop it. A CHECK covers a rule about one row; rules across many rows stay in your code.
The database refuses the state itself, and with Atomicity the transaction's other steps are undone too.

blocks.body: A transaction means: everything happens, or nothing does.

items.meaning: A rule you declare on a table, such as "balance >= 0", which the database checks on every write.

aside.body: A = all or nothing. C = rules stay intact. I = I never see others' half-done work. D = committed means committed.

items: C gets its strength from the constraints you write. Without constraints, the database has no idea which states are "wrong".
Of the four, I is the slippery one: it is not yes or no but a dial with several settings.

check.q: One second after showing "success", the database server crashes. Which ACID letter says the money won't be lost, and how?
check.a: D, Durability. The change is written to the log on disk before the commit is answered, so the database restores it when it restarts.

slides.title: Transactions in Doctrine: flush() and wrapInTransaction()
slides.tldr: flush() is already a transaction; when a job has several steps, locks or raw SQL, wrap the whole job in wrapInTransaction().

blocks.body: In Doctrine, `flush()` is itself a transaction: it sends all pending changes together, and if one fails it rolls everything back. So the first rule is one `flush()` per job, at the very end. When you have to read, take a lock or run raw SQL in the middle, keep the whole job inside `wrapInTransaction()`.

marks.tip: BEGIN happens here. Everything inside (reads, locks, writes) is part of one transaction. Whatever the closure returns is handed back to you.

The deadlock fix. If Ryan to Kevin and Kevin to Ryan run together, a fixed from-then-to order lets each grab one wallet and wait for the other forever. Sorted ids make both queue on the same wallet first.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE: until this transaction commits, no other transaction can change this row. Without it, two transfers could read the same stale balance and compute wrong results.
If an exception escapes from here, wrapInTransaction() issues ROLLBACK itself, so Ryan's debit does not stay behind.
When the closure ends, Doctrine calls flush() itself and then COMMIT. You never write a separate flush().

blocks.title: Three rules
items: No `flush()` calls scattered through service methods; call it once, at the end of the job.
Several steps, a lock, DQL or raw SQL together: use `wrapInTransaction()`.
After an exception the EntityManager is closed. Don't try to write with it again in the same request.

items.meaning: Doctrine's internal ledger: it remembers which entities changed and sends all the SQL together on flush().
Taking a lock on the row while reading it, so nobody else can change it until you commit.

items: Without the sort() above, Ryan→Kevin and Kevin→Ryan at the same time take their two locks in opposite order and deadlock: each waits for the other.
"The EntityManager is closed" means an earlier transaction failed. Finish that request with an error response.
Messenger's `doctrine_transaction` middleware wraps every message handler in a transaction automatically.
Locks make competing transfers on the same wallet wait their turn, so keep the transaction short. For a row nobody else touches, the lock is wasted effort.

check.q: When an exception escapes from the closure of wrapInTransaction(), what does Doctrine do?
check.a: It sends ROLLBACK, so none of the changes are saved. It closes the EntityManager and rethrows the exception, so you can return an error response.

slides.title: Rollback can't take back an email or an SMS
slides.tldr: A transaction only undoes changes in its own database; an SMS, email or HTTP call made inside it stays sent and also holds locks.

blocks.body: A transaction can only undo changes to **its own database**. If you send an SMS, an email or an HTTP call to another service from inside it, that message is already out in the world, and a later rollback won't recall it. Imagine Venmo texting "you have received money" and then canceling the transfer. There is a second danger: while a slow call runs, the transaction stays open, and everyone else queues up behind the locked rows.

marks.tip: If the gateway hangs for 20 seconds, the transaction stays open for 20 seconds, and nobody else can touch these two wallets.
flush() and COMMIT happen after the closure. If a constraint breaks or the connection drops, everything rolls back, but the SMS has already arrived.
If the commit fails, execution never reaches this line, so a wrong SMS can't go out. A worker will call the gateway later.

blocks.body: Inside a transaction, only database work. Anything for the outside world comes after the commit.

items: Writing files, clearing a cache, publishing to a queue, charging a payment gateway: none of these roll back.
If the dispatch fails after the commit, the money is fine and only the SMS is lost. If even that is unacceptable, you need the outbox pattern.

aside.body: Rollback undoes what is inside the database. What has left it has left it.

items.label: Keeping a database and outside services in step

check.q: An SMS is sent from inside the transaction, then COMMIT fails. What does Kevin see, and why?
check.a: He gets the "money received" SMS, but his balance doesn't go up. The database changes were rolled back, while the SMS had already reached an outside system and can't be recalled.

slides.title: What a transaction protects, and what it doesn't
slides.tldr: A transaction stops half-done work and rule violations; it does not stop race conditions, outside services or wrong calculations.

blocks.body: A transaction is powerful, but it isn't magic. Its four promises hold only inside its own database. This is where people get it wrong most often: two transactions can both read Ryan's balance as $500 at the same moment and both deduct $400. Both write back $100, so $800 went out but the balance shows only $400 gone. Each transaction is flawless on its own, yet the result is wrong.

blocks.caption: Where the power of a transaction ends

columns.title: Protects against
items: An error or crash midway: no half-done work is saved
Data that breaks a constraint: it never commits
Other people's uncommitted changes: you don't see them
Power loss after commit: the data survives
columns.tip: These four are direct ACID promises: the database guarantees them itself and you write no extra code.

columns.title: Does not protect against
items: Two transactions reading the same stale value and calculating from it
Email, SMS, HTTP calls: they don't roll back
Data in another database or another service
A wrong calculation in your code: it commits perfectly too
columns.tip: Each of these needs its own technique: locks, atomic updates, the outbox pattern, and tests.

marks.tip: The database does the read and the write as one step, so a second request sees the already reduced balance. The next segments show this and locks in full.

blocks.body: A transaction prevents half-done work; it does not prevent the wrong arithmetic of two simultaneous requests.

aside.body: "I used a transaction, so I'm safe": this belief is the source of double-spend and double-booking bugs. The links below show which tool covers which gap.

items.label: Simultaneous requests: spotting a race condition
Using locks to stop stale reads

check.q: Two transfers both read Ryan's balance as $500 and each deducted $400. Both ran inside transactions, so why is the result still wrong?
check.a: A transaction makes each job indivisible, but at the default isolation level both can read the same stale balance. Preventing that takes a lock or an atomic update.

slides.title: One transaction, two queries, two different truths
slides.tldr: Even inside one transaction, another commit can slip in between two queries; the isolation level decides how much gets in.

blocks.body: The Miller Market's monthly report says "total outstanding: $500" on the first page, yet the list below it adds up to $400. Both queries ran inside the same transaction. But in the gap between them, Kevin's $100 payment was committed, and the second query saw it. So where did the I in ACID go? The answer: isolation isn't a switch, it's a dial with four settings, and the default setting is fairly loose. The fix is one line, shown below: ask for REPEATABLE READ, so the whole transaction works from one snapshot, a frozen picture taken when it starts. The price: the report shows the shop as of its start, so Kevin's payment appears only in the next run.

marks.tip: It saw whatever was committed at the moment this query ran: total outstanding $500.
This query looked at the database afresh. Kevin's payment had been committed by then, so the rows add up to $400.

blocks.caption: A payment slips in between the report's two queries

actors.label: Report
actors.tip: Runs two queries inside one transaction: the total first, then the list.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: At READ COMMITTED, it shows each query the data that was committed at that moment.

actors.label: Kevin's payment
actors.tip: A completely separate request that reduces Kevin's $100 due in its own transaction.

messages.label: Kevin's due −$100, commit
messages.tip: The report's transaction is still open, yet nothing stops this commit.

messages.label: List: sums to $400
messages.tip: The second query saw the new state. Two queries in one transaction got pictures from two different moments.
The report disagrees with itself. No error, no log entry, just a wrong sheet of paper.

marks.tip: PostgreSQL: this must run before the transaction's first query, and it applies to this one transaction only.
Both queries read the same frozen picture, so the total and the list agree: $500 and $500.

items.meaning: How much of each other's changes concurrent transactions are allowed to see.
A strange, wrong result that appears because isolation is loose.

aside.body: Being inside a transaction doesn't mean you are alone. The isolation level decides how alone you are.

check.q: Both queries were in the same transaction, so why didn't the numbers match?
check.a: At the default READ COMMITTED level, each query sees the data committed at the moment it runs. Kevin's payment was committed between the two queries, so the second one saw the new state.

slides.title: Three read problems: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom
slides.tldr: Dirty read = reading unconfirmed writes; non-repeatable = a row you read changes; phantom = new rows appear.

blocks.title: The credit ledger: pencil and pen
blocks.body: In a store's house-account ledger, the clerk first writes in pencil (not yet committed). Once the figures check out, he goes over it in pen (commit); if they don't, he erases it (rollback). You stand beside him reading the ledger. Which entries you may see, and whether you see the same thing when you look twice, is exactly what isolation decides.

blocks.caption: The three read anomalies, in ledger terms

cells: You read a pencil entry, then it gets erased
You acted on something that never existed
rows.tip: Reading another transaction's uncommitted change. If it rolls back, you have made a decision on data that was never true.

cells: You read the same line twice; someone inked over it in between
Two different values for the same row
rows.tip: Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting two values, because another transaction changed it and committed in between.

cells: You count lines matching a rule twice; a new line appeared in between
rows.tip: Running the same WHERE query twice and getting extra rows (or missing ones) the second time, because someone committed an INSERT or DELETE in between.

blocks.body: All three are **read** problems: you didn't corrupt anything, you just looked at a wrong or shifting picture. They bite in reports, reconciliations, and any code that says "count first, then decide".

aside.body: Dirty = reading pencil. Non-repeatable = an old line changes. Phantom = a new line sprouts.

items: PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads: even if you ask for READ UNCOMMITTED, it behaves like READ COMMITTED.
The report problem on the previous slide is a close cousin of the non-repeatable read: two queries saw pictures from two moments.

check.q: What is the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom read?
check.a: In a non-repeatable read, the value of a row you already read changes. In a phantom, running the same query again shows new rows, or earlier rows vanish.

slides.title: Two write problems: lost update and write skew
slides.tldr: In a lost update, a write to the same row disappears; in write skew, two valid writes to different rows together break a rule.

blocks.body: Read problems make a report wrong; write problems corrupt the data itself. **Lost update**: two clerks read the same line, each calculates on their own and writes back, and the second wipes out the first. **Write skew** is subtler. The shop's rule is that at least one person must be on duty. Jason and Chris both look at the ledger, see "2 on duty", and each writes leave on **their own** line.

blocks.caption: Write skew: both read correctly, both wrote validly, yet nobody is minding the shop

actors.label: Jason
actors.tip: Wants leave. Follows the rule by first checking that someone else is on duty.

actors.label: Duty ledger
actors.tip: The shift table: one row per employee, with on_duty true or false.

actors.label: Chris
actors.tip: At exactly the same moment, runs the same check and reaches the same decision.

messages.label: 2 people
messages.tip: Jason hasn't written anything yet, so Chris sees 2 too.

messages.label: My row: on leave
messages.tip: He changed only his own row. Looked at alone, this is perfectly valid.

messages.label: My row: on leave
messages.tip: A different row, so it doesn't collide with Jason's write. Neither a row lock nor a version column notices anything.
No write was lost and no error was raised. What got damaged is the rule both of them checked at the start.

blocks.caption: The two problems side by side

columns.title: Lost update
items: Two people read the same row and write the same row
Due is $50; both add $10 and write $60, instead of $70
Prevented by: atomic UPDATE (SET due = due + 100), FOR UPDATE lock, version column
columns.tip: Happens in read-modify-write code: read, calculate in PHP, write. Fairly easy to recognize and to prevent.

columns.title: Write skew
items: Two people read the same facts and write different rows
Both take leave, so nobody is on duty
Prevented by: SERIALIZABLE level, or locking what you read to decide
columns.tip: Happens when the rule spans several rows ("at least one", "at most 10 in total"). The hardest to catch.

aside.body: There are plenty of tools against lost updates. Write skew is hard to catch because the two transactions touch different rows, so ordinary row locks and optimistic version checks raise no objection.

items.label: Stopping lost updates with an atomic UPDATE

check.q: What sets write skew apart from a lost update?
check.a: In a lost update, two transactions write the same row and one wipes out the other. In write skew they write different rows; no write is lost, but together they break a rule both checked at the start.

slides.title: The four levels: which one stops which problem
slides.tldr: Read uncommitted → read committed → repeatable read → serializable: the higher you go, the fewer anomalies, but the more waiting and aborted transactions.

blocks.title: Four rules for reading the ledger
blocks.body: The four levels are four rules for reading the credit ledger. The stricter the rule, the fewer the surprises, but the more waiting and "do it again".

items: **Read uncommitted**: read the pencil entries too.
**Read committed**: only pen entries, but every query looks at the ledger afresh.
**Repeatable read**: photocopy the ledger up front (a snapshot) and work from that copy for the whole transaction.
**Serializable**: the result must look as if everyone had taken the ledger one at a time.

blocks.caption: Which anomaly happens at which level, and which is prevented

rows.tip: Happens only at the lowest level. Not even there in PostgreSQL: if you ask for READ UNCOMMITTED, it behaves like READ COMMITTED.
From REPEATABLE READ on, the whole transaction sees one snapshot, so reading the same row again gives the same value.
The SQL standard allows phantoms at REPEATABLE READ. In practice PostgreSQL's snapshot shows none, and neither does MySQL InnoDB for plain SELECTs.
PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ aborts the second writer with an error, so nothing is lost. In MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ, a later UPDATE silently overwrites the earlier one.
The two transactions write different rows, so a snapshot notices nothing. Only SERIALIZABLE connects the reads and writes of both and aborts one of them.

blocks.body: The default level is not SERIALIZABLE. Unless you take extra measures, lost updates and write skew are not being prevented.

items: Defaults: PostgreSQL = READ COMMITTED, MySQL (InnoDB) = REPEATABLE READ. Neither is SERIALIZABLE.
Levels with the same name behave differently across databases. Read your own database's documentation once.

items.meaning: A frozen picture of the data as of the start of the transaction; whatever others commit later, you keep seeing that picture.
The database realized the result wouldn't match "one at a time" and aborted the transaction (SQLSTATE 40001).

check.q: Of the five anomalies, which one never happens at PostgreSQL's default level, and which ones can?
check.a: The default READ COMMITTED prevents only dirty reads. Non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update and write skew can all happen.

slides.title: When to raise the level, and why you must retry
slides.tldr: Keep the default level; when a rule spans several rows, make just that one transaction SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failure.

blocks.body: Most work stays at the default level, and each specific problem has its own specific tool. Where a rule **spans several rows**, such as "at least one person on duty", make only that transaction SERIALIZABLE. It comes at a price: when the database detects a collision, it aborts one transaction. That's not a bug but normal behavior, and rerunning the whole transaction usually succeeds.

marks.tip: The level changes for this one transaction only; the rest of the app stays at the default. It must run before the transaction's first query.
Doctrine DBAL surfaces both serialization failures (40001) and deadlocks as exceptions implementing RetryableException. Other exceptions aren't caught, because they are real bugs.
A short random pause (jitter), so two colliding transactions don't fire again at exactly the same moment.
It's fine if Jason and Chris both read 2 here: at commit time the database aborts one of them, and on retry he reads 1 and stops.

blocks.title: Which tool for which problem
items: Single-row arithmetic (stock, balance): an atomic UPDATE or a lock; no need to change the level.
A long report that needs one picture for all its queries: REPEATABLE READ (read-only, so no aborts; it shows data as of its start).
A rule spanning several rows (write skew): SERIALIZABLE plus retry.

blocks.body: SERIALIZABLE promises "no wrong results", not "no aborts". Without retry it is incomplete.

items: Don't make SERIALIZABLE the default for the whole app: more aborts and retries will slow it down.
Keep emails, HTTP calls and queue dispatches out of the retried closure, because it may run several times.
If a transaction is already open outside, SET TRANSACTION fails; call the runner from the outermost layer.
In PostgreSQL, a REPEATABLE READ transaction that writes can also be aborted if it touches a row someone else changed. Read-only reports never are.
In MySQL, run `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL …` before the transaction starts; it then applies only to the next transaction.

items.label: Solving the same problem with locks

check.q: What extra piece must your code have when using SERIALIZABLE, and why?
check.a: Retry. When the database detects a collision, it aborts one transaction with a serialization failure. That is normal behavior, not a bug, and rerunning the whole transaction usually succeeds.

slides.title: Two phones, one balance, spent twice
slides.tldr: When two requests read the same stale balance at once, both pass the check, and money that doesn't exist gets spent.

blocks.body: Ryan has $1,000 in his wallet. From two phones, within the same second, he sends $800 each time. The code does check the balance on every request, yet both transfers succeed. Testing alone will never catch this, because the bug only appears when the **timing of two requests lines up**. The fix, shown below the diagram, is to let the database check and subtract in one statement.

marks.tip: Both requests see 1000 here. Nobody has written anything yet, so both conclude "there is enough money".
Both write 1000 − 800 = 200. The second write silently wipes out the first.

blocks.caption: Ryan's two phones read the same balance, and $800 leaves twice

actors.label: Ryan's phone 1
actors.tip: First request: send $800.

actors.label: Ryan's phone 2
actors.tip: Second request: send $800 again, at almost the same moment.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Ryan's wallet row holds a balance of $1,000.

messages.label: Read the balance
messages.tip: SELECT balance. There is no lock, so nobody blocks anybody.

messages.label: Read the balance
messages.tip: The first request hasn't written yet, so this one gets the stale value too.

messages.label: balance = 1000 − 800 = 200
messages.tip: Phone 2 has no idea phone 1 already changed the balance.
Correctly, the second transfer should have failed. $600 was created out of thin air.

marks.tip: The WHERE is the check, the SET is the write. The database does both on one row, one request at a time, so phone 2 finds $200 < $800 and matches nothing.
0 rows changed means the check failed. Phone 1 changed 1 row and succeeded; phone 2 changed 0 and is refused.

aside.title: The coupon on campaign night
aside.body: An app offered "$10 off your first order", once per user. On the night of the offer, some users double-tapped the button, and others tapped again because the network looked slow. By morning, about a hundred users had received the coupon twice.

items.meaning: A bug where the result depends on how two operations happen to be timed: fine when run alone, wrong when run together.
The same money being spent twice.

items.label: Atomic updates in depth, and where they stop working
Locks, for decisions that span several rows

check.q: Both requests ran exactly as the code says, so why is the balance wrong?
check.a: Both read the same stale balance before either wrote. The other request slipped into the gap between the check and the write.

slides.title: Where the gap is: check-then-act and read-modify-write
slides.tldr: Nearly every race condition has the same shape: read something, think, then write, and someone else can get in between the read and the write.

blocks.title: The grocery store's stock ledger
blocks.body: A grocery store keeps one ledger, and two clerks use it. Both look and see "rice: 10 lb in stock". Each sells 8 lb and writes "2 lb". The store actually has −6 lb of rice. Neither clerk made a mistake; the trouble is that a second clerk read the ledger between the first one's look and his write.

blocks.caption: One gap, four faces
headers: What it looks like in code

cells: One statement that checks and acts, or lock first
rows.tip: The state can change after the condition is checked, but the code carries on as if the earlier look were still true.

cells: Counter or stock updates are lost
rows.tip: Two requests read the same value and each writes its own result; the last write wipes out the earlier one. This is called a lost update.

cells: Money that doesn't exist gets spent
rows.tip: The money version of check-then-act. Wallets, points, credits, coupons: it is the same everywhere.

cells: Check a seat or slot, then take it
One thing assigned to two people
Unique constraint on the seat or slot
rows.tip: Seats, doctor slots, meeting rooms, delivery slots: anything meant for one person can suffer this.

blocks.body: Another request can get in between the read and the write.

aside.body: Look-then-do in two steps means a gap. Close the gap, or merge the two steps into one.
The gap lasts milliseconds, so with low traffic it hits once a year. With heavy traffic or retries it hits daily, and that is when it is hardest to catch.

items.label: What a transaction does not protect

check.q: The counter code `$n = $row->count; $row->count = $n + 1;` is which kind of race, and why?
check.a: Read-modify-write. Two requests read the same `$n` and both write `$n + 1`, so the counter goes up once where it should have gone up twice.

slides.title: How to catch a race condition in your own code
slides.tldr: Be suspicious of any read-then-write in code, then fire 20 identical requests at once and check the result.

blocks.title: Smells to look for in code review
items: A `find` or `findOneBy`, then an `if`, then `persist` or a setter.
Reading a value with a getter, doing arithmetic, and passing it back to a setter: `setStock($s->getStock() - 1)`.
"Check if it exists, create it if not" code.
A comment beside the code saying "two people won't do this at once". They will.

blocks.body: If you suspect a race, prove it. Send many identical requests at the same time, then reconcile the numbers in the database. If you fire twenty $100 transfers at once from a $1,000 wallet, exactly 10 should succeed. If more than 10 succeed, or the balance isn't 0, there is a race. After you fix the code, run the same script again: exactly 10 successes and a balance of 0 is your proof.

blocks.code:
# 20 requests, with up to 20 running at the same time
seq 1 20 | xargs -P 20 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
  -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/wallets/1/send \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"amount": 100}' | sort | uniq -c

# then reconcile the numbers
psql app -c "SELECT balance FROM wallet WHERE id = 1;"

marks.tip: -P 20 means 20 curl processes run at once. Run them one after another and you will never see the race.
With correct code, balance = 0 and there are exactly 10 responses with status 200. A negative balance or more than 10 successes means you caught a race.

items: In development, add an artificial `usleep(200000)` between the read and the write. The gap widens and the race becomes easy to see. Remove it afterwards.
Tests like this are easier as a separate script or with k6 than in PHPUnit, because you need genuinely parallel HTTP requests.

items.desc: runs 20 processes at the same time
counts how many times each status appeared

check.q: You fire twenty $100 transfers at once at a $1,000 wallet and 12 succeed. What does that tell you?
check.a: There is a race condition. At most 10 should succeed; 12 successes means some requests passed the check on the same stale balance.

slides.title: The "check if it exists first" trap, and its fix
slides.tldr: Searching before inserting a new row races; the real guard is the database's unique constraint, and you handle its exception.

blocks.body: The most familiar race is "check whether anyone has already registered with this email, and if not, create a new account". If another request slips in between the check and the insert, two accounts get created. Your application code is fine at **checking** here, but it can't **guard**. Only the database can guard, because it lines every request up in a single queue.

marks.tip: If two requests hear "none" at the same moment, both carry on. This if guarantees nothing.
This constraint lives inside the database. Even if two requests arrive together, only one insert survives.
The losing request gets an exception from the database; turn it into a friendly error for the user. The EntityManager is closed after this, so the next request starts fresh.

blocks.body: The app can't fix this, the database can: add a unique constraint to stop duplicates.

items: A PHP static variable, a file flag or a session lock can't stop this race. With several servers or workers, they never see each other.
Disabling the button is only UX. It does nothing when someone sends the request straight with curl, or when a retry happens.
A unique constraint only stops duplicates. A rule like "balance never below 0" needs an atomic UPDATE or a lock instead.

check.q: Two accounts were created despite the email-exists `if`. What one thing would have prevented it properly?
check.a: A unique constraint on the email column. When two inserts arrive together, one fails, and you catch that exception to tell the user "email already taken".

slides.title: Pessimistic lock: take the key, everyone else queues
slides.tldr: SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the row as you read it; the second request waits in line and then reads the correct balance.

blocks.title: The key to the bank vault
blocks.body: There is only one key to the vault. Whoever goes in with it works while everyone else queues outside until they are done. That is a pessimistic lock: "I assume trouble will happen, so I lock up first". Ryan's two phone requests now stand in that queue, and the second one walks in later to see a clean, up-to-date balance.

blocks.caption: FOR UPDATE: the second request waits until the first one commits

actors.label: Ryan's phone 1
actors.tip: The first request, wanting to send $800.

actors.label: Ryan's phone 2
actors.tip: The second request, which arrived at almost the same moment.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Manages the row lock on the wallet row.

messages.label: SELECT … FOR UPDATE
messages.tip: It gets the row's lock together with the read.

messages.label: SELECT … FOR UPDATE
messages.tip: The row is locked, so this query simply hangs. No error is raised; it just waits.

messages.label: Write balance $200, COMMIT
messages.tip: The lock is released the moment the commit happens.

messages.label: $200, lock granted
messages.tip: Now phone 2 sees the new balance.

messages.label: $200 < $800, abort
messages.tip: The second transfer fails exactly as it should. No wrong money went out.

blocks.body: Take the lock, then read. Taking the lock after you have read is too late.

aside.body: The simplest way to close the check-then-act gap: lock the row you are going to decide on before you decide. When collisions are frequent, this is the right choice.

items.meaning: A lock on one row; other transactions cannot change it (or read it with FOR UPDATE) until it is released.
Assuming up front that a collision will happen, so locking first.

use: Frequent collisions on one row: wallet, stock, the last seat
Short work between the read and the write
avoid: The user thinks for minutes between read and write (a form)
Slow calls would end up inside the lock

check.q: Until phone 1's transaction commits, what does phone 2's `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` do?
check.a: It blocks and waits; it does not raise an error. When phone 1 commits, the lock is released and phone 2 reads the new balance.

slides.title: PESSIMISTIC_WRITE in Doctrine: rules and time limits
slides.tldr: Pass PESSIMISTIC_WRITE to find() inside an open transaction, keep the work short, and put a cap on the waiting time.

blocks.body: In Doctrine, passing `LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` as the third argument of `find()` adds `FOR UPDATE` to the SQL. It only works inside an open transaction; otherwise you get a `TransactionRequiredException`. So wrap the whole job in `wrapInTransaction()`. The shorter you hold the lock, the shorter the queue.

marks.tip: SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Outside a transaction, this raises a TransactionRequiredException.
This if is now safe, because the row is held under our lock. No other request can get in here.
The lock is released on commit or rollback, whichever happens. There is no way to unlock it earlier by hand.
Without lock_timeout, one hung transaction can block everyone else indefinitely. In MySQL, innodb_lock_wait_timeout does this job.
SKIP LOCKED doesn't wait; it steps over rows that are locked. It lets several workers pick different jobs from the same table.

items: No HTTP calls, SMS or other slow work inside a lock. The lock lasts as long as the queue does.
Lock only the rows your decision depends on. Locking a whole table puts everyone in the queue.

items.meaning: In ORM 3 it is `Doctrine\DBAL\LockMode`. PESSIMISTIC_WRITE means FOR UPDATE; PESSIMISTIC_READ means a shared lock.

check.q: What happens if you call `find($class, $id, LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` without a transaction, and when is the lock released?
check.a: You get a TransactionRequiredException, because the lock only works in an open transaction. The lock is released when the transaction commits or rolls back.

slides.title: Optimistic lock: don't hold anything, check the seal on the way out
slides.tldr: Keep a version column on the row; the UPDATE applies only if the version is still what it was; otherwise the conflict is caught.

blocks.body: Two admins open the same product form, and one of them takes 10 minutes to fill it in. You can't hold a database lock for 10 minutes, yet you can't let one admin's work silently vanish either. This is where an optimistic lock helps: everyone gets in, but on the way out the seal number on the vault is compared. If the number has changed, someone else worked in the meantime. When to pick this over a pessimistic lock is the next slide.

blocks.caption: Two admins open the form at version 3; the second one's save is caught

actors.label: Admin Sarah
actors.tip: Is changing the product's name.

actors.label: Admin Rob
actors.tip: Is changing the same product's price. Opened the form at the same time as Sarah.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Keeps a version column on the product row.

messages.label: save, expecting version = 3
messages.tip: The version received when the form was opened is sent back.

messages.label: OK, now version 4
messages.tip: UPDATE … SET version = 4 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3 changed one row.

messages.label: save, expecting version = 3
messages.tip: Rob still holds the old 3.
Zero rows changed; Doctrine sees this and throws an OptimisticLockException.

messages.label: 409 Conflict
messages.tip: Rob didn't destroy Sarah's change. He is told to reload and look again.

marks.tip: Doctrine bumps the version on every UPDATE and checks it in the WHERE clause itself. You write no code for it.
If the version the client sent back doesn't match the row's current version, the exception is thrown right here.

items: In a JSON API, send the version in the body or in an ETag/If-Match header; return 412 or 409 on a mismatch.
On a conflict, show the client the fresh data and let them resolve it. Quietly forcing the write through is a lost update all over again.

use: Collisions are rare, but users work in a form for a long time
Editing the same record in an admin panel
avoid: Frequently contended figures such as wallet or stock, where retries pile up

check.q: How does the database know there was a conflict when the second admin saves?
check.a: The UPDATE's WHERE clause says `version = 3`, but the row is already at version 4. Zero rows change, and Doctrine throws an OptimisticLockException.

slides.title: Which lock? One rule to choose
slides.tldr: Rare collisions and slow humans: optimistic. Frequent collisions and quick code: pessimistic. A plain counter needs neither: one atomic UPDATE does it.

blocks.body: Ask two questions. How often do two requests really touch the same row at the same moment? And how long must the row be held between the read and the write? Two admins editing the same product in the same ten minutes is rare, maybe 1 save in 500. A hundred buyers chasing the last 50 tickets collide on nearly every request. Heavy collisions make an optimistic lock fail and retry again and again. And a pessimistic lock on a form left open for minutes makes everyone queue behind one sleepy admin.

blocks.caption: Optimistic or pessimistic: decide by collision rate and how long the work takes

rows.tip: The thresholds are a rule of thumb. What matters is that one is "almost never" and the other is "all the time".

cells: Long: a form open for minutes
rows.tip: You cannot hold a database lock while a person types, but you can while a function runs.

cells: Nothing is held; others carry on
The row is locked; others queue
rows.tip: This is why the optimistic one suits slow work: nobody waits for the person filling the form.

cells: Gets an error, reloads, redoes the work
Waits its turn, then reads fresh data
rows.tip: With an optimistic lock the loser's work is thrown away. With a pessimistic lock it just waits.

cells: Retries pile up if collisions are common
Queues, deadlock risk, slow if held long
rows.tip: Each approach hurts exactly where the other is comfortable. Pick the one whose price you can afford.

cells: Wallet balance, stock, the last seat
rows.tip: Think of who is colliding: a few humans taking turns, or a crowd hitting one number.

blocks.body: Rare collisions and slow people: optimistic. Frequent collisions and quick code: pessimistic.

items: If all you do is add or subtract a number (stock, a counter), skip both: one `UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0` is atomic on its own.
The numbers are a rule of thumb, not a law. Count the OptimisticLockExceptions in your logs; if more than 1 in 20 saves hits one, move that screen to a pessimistic lock.

items.label: Atomic updates with no lock at all

check.q: A shop has 50 tickets and 200 people click Buy in the first second. Which lock, and why?
check.a: Pessimistic (or one atomic UPDATE on the stock). Nearly every request collides, so an optimistic lock would fail and retry over and over. The work is short, so queueing for the row is cheap.

slides.title: Advisory locks and Symfony Lock: a lock with no row
slides.tldr: You can lock a name instead of a row. It suits cron jobs, exports and multi-server work, but the TTL has a trap.

blocks.body: There isn't always a row to lock: for example, "the monthly invoice export must run only once". Then you lock a name. Inside the database, that's an advisory lock (`pg_advisory_xact_lock` in PostgreSQL). Across several servers or outside the database, use Symfony Lock, backed by Redis or a database. Such locks have a **TTL** (time to live), meaning they release themselves when the time runs out.

marks.tip: A lock by name. Without a TTL, a crashed process would hold the lock forever, which is why there is one.
acquire() returns false immediately instead of waiting. Pass acquire(true) if you want it to wait.
In long jobs, call refresh() now and then, or the TTL expires mid-job and someone else walks in.
It is released automatically on COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so you can't forget to release it. It works even with no row or table involved.
This is what guards correctness. Even if the TTL lock is lost and two exports start, the database refuses the second one.

blocks.body: A lock with a TTL is for efficiency only; correctness of money is guarded by a database constraint.

items: Say the TTL is 120 seconds and the job freezes for 150 (a long GC pause, a slow disk). The lock expires at 120, a second server takes it, and now both run.
If a Redis node is lost or fails over, the lock can vanish. Don't rely on it alone for the correctness of money.

check.q: A Symfony Lock has a 60-second TTL but the job takes 90 seconds. What can go wrong, and how do you avoid it?
check.a: When the TTL runs out the lock releases itself, someone else walks in, and two run at once. Call `refresh()` during the job, and keep a database constraint for correctness.

slides.title: Deadlock: each waiting for the other
slides.tldr: When two transactions take locks in opposite order, both get stuck; always lock in the same order, and retry when a deadlock error occurs.

blocks.body: Ryan is sending money to Kevin, and at the very same moment Kevin is sending money to Ryan. The first transaction locks Ryan's wallet first, the second locks Kevin's. Now the first wants Kevin's and the second wants Ryan's. Neither will let go, so the database aborts one of them itself.

blocks.caption: Locking in opposite order leaves the two transfers stuck

actors.label: Ryan → Kevin
actors.tip: Locks its own wallet first, then the recipient's.

actors.label: Kevin → Ryan
actors.tip: Locks its own wallet first (Kevin's), then Ryan's.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Keeps a graph of who waits for whom, and aborts one transaction when it finds a cycle.

messages.label: Wants Kevin's wallet
messages.tip: Kevin's is held by t2, so t1 waits.

messages.label: Wants Ryan's wallet
messages.tip: Ryan's is held by t1, so t2 waits too.

messages.note: Cycle: each waits for the other
messages.tip: This is a deadlock. If nobody gave way, they would be stuck forever.

messages.label: Deadlock! You are aborted
messages.tip: The database rolls back one transaction. The other moves on.

marks.tip: Transfers in both directions now lock the smaller id first, so nobody waits in opposite order. A cycle cannot form.
Keep this code the same everywhere. If the order is wrong in even one place, deadlocks come back.
Only a deadlock is retried. Any other error, such as insufficient funds, is a real failure and goes up.
After an exception, wrapInTransaction() closes the EntityManager. resetManager() gives a fresh one.
A random wait, so the two collided transfers don't restart in lockstep and collide again.

items: After a deadlock the database aborts one transaction and you get a DeadlockException. Retry the whole transaction from the start, as above, or let a Messenger retry do it.
Cap the retries (here 3) and add the random wait, or two transactions restart at the same moment and collide again.

aside.body: When you need several locks, always take them in the same order: smaller id first.

items.label: Atomic updates with no lock at all

check.q: Why do two transfers in opposite directions deadlock, and which rule stops it?
check.a: One transaction holds Ryan's wallet and wants Kevin's, while the other does the reverse. If every transaction locks in the same order (smaller id first), such a cycle can never form.

slides.title: The last phone, sold to two people
slides.tldr: Put the condition and the change in one SQL statement and the database closes the gap itself: UPDATE … WHERE stock >= n, then check how many rows changed.

blocks.title: The host's reserved card
blocks.body: A restaurant host puts a "reserved" card on a table: looking and placing the card happen in one motion. If it took three steps ("see if the table is free, think about it, then place the card"), another party could sit down in the middle. An atomic operation is exactly that one motion: checking the condition and making the change happen in a single database step.

blocks.code:
$p = $em->find(Product::class, $id);      // both requests read stock = 1
if ($p->getStock() >= 1) {                // both pass the check
    $p->setStock($p->getStock() - 1);     // both write 0
    $em->flush();                         // two orders confirmed, one phone
}

marks.tip: The read happens in one step and the write in another. Kevin's request can read in the gap, and still sees 1.
Nothing fails: 0 is a perfectly legal stock value, so the database accepts both writes. Hence a plain CHECK would not catch this either.

blocks.caption: One phone in stock, two buyers at once. With a single UPDATE, only one gets it

actors.label: Ryan's order
actors.tip: Wants to buy the last phone.

actors.label: Kevin's order
actors.tip: Wants to buy the same phone at almost the same moment.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: The product row has stock = 1.

messages.label: stock = stock − 1 WHERE stock >= 1
messages.tip: The condition and the change are in one statement. The database locks the row while it does it.

messages.label: 1 row changed
messages.tip: affected rows = 1 means Ryan got it.

messages.label: stock = stock − 1 WHERE stock >= 1
messages.tip: Now stock is 0, so the WHERE doesn't match.

messages.label: 0 rows changed
messages.tip: affected rows = 0 means sold out. Kevin is told "it's gone".
There was no gap, so there is no overselling either.

blocks.body: Put the condition in the WHERE, then check how many rows changed.

aside.body: "Read, think, write" takes three steps. When one SQL statement holds both the condition and the change, the database locks the row itself, so there is no gap.

items.meaning: One indivisible step: nobody else can get in the middle.
The number of rows an UPDATE or DELETE actually changed.

check.q: Two requests run `UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1` at once, with stock at 1. Who gets what?
check.a: One gets affected rows = 1 (and the phone); the other gets 0 (sold out). stock never goes negative.

slides.title: Atomic UPDATE in Symfony: DQL and DBAL
slides.tldr: Instead of getter and setter, run `SET stock = stock - :n WHERE … AND stock >= :n` through DQL or DBAL; a result of 0 means no stock.

blocks.body: In Doctrine, the easiest route is a bulk `UPDATE` in DQL. `execute()` returns how many rows changed, and that number is itself the answer to "did the condition match?". If it is 0, throw an exception, and stock can never go negative.

marks.tip: The arithmetic happens in the database, not in PHP, so it never gets mixed up with another request.
The condition and the change are in the same statement. This `p.stock >= :qty` is what prevents overselling.
0 means someone took the stock earlier. Handle it as a business error, not a bug.
The CHECK constraint is the final guard. Even if some other code or script makes a mistake, it is stopped here.

items: A DQL bulk UPDATE bypasses the Unit of Work; a `$product` loaded earlier will show the old stock, so call `$em->refresh($product)`. If you use #[ORM\Version], also write `p.version = p.version + 1`.
There is no point if you don't look at the result of `execute()`; if the code carries on after a 0, you get the same oversell.

use: One row and one condition: stock, counters, status changes.
avoid: A rule spanning several tables or needing a long calculation: lock the rows inside a transaction instead.

items: Without Doctrine, running SQL directly with `$connection->executeStatement($sql, $params)` returns the same number.

check.q: After a DQL bulk UPDATE, does a `$product->getStock()` loaded earlier give the right value?
check.a: No, it still gives the old value, because a bulk UPDATE bypasses the Unit of Work. Call `$em->refresh($product)` if you need the new value.

slides.title: Compare-and-swap: "is it still in the state I expect?"
slides.tldr: Put the old state in the UPDATE's WHERE (status = 'pending'); affected rows 1 means you won, 0 means someone else got there first.

blocks.body: Compare-and-swap (CAS) means: "only put in the new value if the current value is what I think it is". In SQL, that is `WHERE status = 'pending'`. When the same payment's webhook arrives twice, a plain "read status, then mark paid" lets both pass, and the customer gets two receipts. With CAS the database lets only one win, and only the winner sends the receipt.

blocks.caption: Two webhooks for the same payment: only the first sends a receipt

actors.label: webhook 1
actors.tip: The first message from the payment gateway.

actors.label: webhook 2
actors.tip: A gateway retry or duplicate message, arriving at almost the same time.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Order 12's status is currently pending.

messages.label: If pending, mark paid
messages.tip: UPDATE … SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 12 AND status = 'pending'.

messages.label: 1 row changed
messages.tip: w1 won. From now on, only it does the receipt work.

messages.label: If pending, mark paid
messages.tip: By the time this UPDATE runs, status is already paid, so the WHERE doesn't match.

messages.label: 0 rows changed
messages.tip: w2 realizes the work has already been done, and just quietly returns 200.

blocks.code:
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'paid', paid_at = NOW()
WHERE id = 12 AND status = 'pending';
-- affected rows = 1 → I won; 0 → someone else got there first

marks.tip: This `status = pending` part is the compare. If the old state doesn't match, nothing changes.
The loser must not return an error: the gateway would only retry again. Reply 200 so it stops.
Receipt, stock and emails belong after this line, so they run exactly once.

aside.body: Put the old state in the WHERE, then count affected rows: 1 means you won.

check.q: Two webhooks both try to mark an order paid with `WHERE status = 'pending'`. How do you tell which one won?
check.a: Look at affected rows. The one with 1 won and sends the receipt; the one with 0 finds the work already done and quietly steps aside.

slides.title: Unique constraints and upsert: keep the rule in the database
slides.tldr: Write the uniqueness rule as an index and the database blocks duplicates itself; upsert does "create if missing, update if present" in one statement.

blocks.body: A unique index isn't only a performance tool, it's a correctness tool. The rule "a user votes only once in a poll" doesn't belong in an `if` in your code: a double tap sends two requests, both find no vote yet, and both insert. Write it as `UNIQUE (poll_id, user_id)` instead. And instead of the two-step "check whether it exists first", use an **upsert**: create if missing, update if present, all in one statement.

blocks.caption: When a rule becomes an index in the database

rows.tip: Two accounts cannot share one email, even when two requests arrive together.
The pair of columns is unique. Even a double tap leaves just one row.

cells: Only one active booking per seat
rows.tip: A partial unique index (PostgreSQL). There can be many canceled bookings, but only one active.

cells: The same idempotency key only once
rows.tip: On a retry, the second insert fails; you can then simply return the earlier response.

blocks.code:
-- PostgreSQL: counting page views, with no race
INSERT INTO page_view (page_id, day, views)
VALUES (7, CURRENT_DATE, 1)
ON CONFLICT (page_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET views = page_view.views + 1;

-- The same thing in MySQL
INSERT INTO page_view (page_id, day, views) VALUES (7, CURDATE(), 1)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE views = views + 1;

marks.tip: The conflict is detected on this unique pair of columns. Without that index, upsert doesn't work.
On a conflict, no new row is made; the existing one gets +1. There is no read in between, so there is no race.

blocks.body: A rule that must never be broken should live in the database, as a unique index or a CHECK.

items: If you only want to know whether it already exists, use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (`INSERT IGNORE` in MySQL) and look at affected rows.
A unique index costs a little on every insert, and the losing insert throws UniqueConstraintViolationException: catch it and show a friendly message.
Doctrine ORM has no built-in upsert; for this, run native SQL through `$connection->executeStatement()`.

check.q: To count daily page views, what do you use instead of the two-step "check if it exists, +1 if so, create if not", and why?
check.a: An upsert (`ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET views = views + 1`). The unique index funnels every request onto one row, and the +1 happens inside the database, so there is no gap.

slides.title: Atomic doesn't help if you ignore the result
slides.tldr: If you run an atomic UPDATE and never look at affected rows, the code assumes it always won and completes the order even on 0.

blocks.body: Plenty of people write the atomic UPDATE correctly, then throw its result away. The database did keep `stock` from going negative, yet the code marks the order "confirmed", because it never learned that the UPDATE changed nothing. The buyer thinks the phone is coming, and there is no phone in stock.

marks.tip: A returned 0 means there was no stock, but the code never looks at it.
This is where the oversell begins. The UPDATE was safe, but the code is blind.
Stock change and order confirmation commit together or not at all, so stock can't drop without an order.
If the result is 0, stop right here. Decide before doing the rest of the work.

items: When there are several steps (reducing stock, creating the order, deducting points), keep them all inside wrapInTransaction(), or stock may drop without any order being created.

In MySQL, affected rows by default counts rows that actually changed, so an UPDATE that leaves a value unchanged reports 0. That isn't an issue when decrementing stock, but remember it for other jobs.

check.q: The UPDATE is safe, so why did the bad code above still oversell?
check.a: The code never looked at the UPDATE's result (the number of rows changed). A 0 meant there was no stock, but the code confirmed the order anyway.

slides.title: The 10 minutes of payment: whose seat is it?
slides.tldr: If you don't hold the seat before payment, people pay and then hear "sold out"; if you hold it with no release, it stays blocked forever. The fix: a hold with a time limit.

blocks.title: The 10 minutes on an online concert ticket
blocks.body: When you pick a seat while buying an online concert ticket, it is held in your name for 10 minutes. Nobody else can take it in that time. If you haven't paid within 10 minutes, the seat becomes free again. That is a hold: a claim, but with an expiry date.

blocks.caption: Three ways to handle a seat during payment

columns.title: Book after payment
items: The seat stays open during payment
Pay, then hear "sold out"
The hassle of a refund
columns.tip: The user finds out the seat is gone only after paying. The worst experience, plus the hassle of a refund.

columns.title: Hold it, never release
items: Seats stuck in abandoned carts
The seat is free but shows "sold out"
Sales drop
columns.tip: The seat is held, but for everyone who left without paying, it stays blocked forever.

columns.title: Hold with expiry
items: Nobody pays and then has to turn back
Unused holds release on their own
The seat is on sale the whole time
columns.tip: The seat is guaranteed while the payment happens, and frees itself when time runs out. Both problems solved.

aside.title: The morning the concert tickets go on sale
aside.body: Someone picks four seats, gets a phone call, and never pays, while hundreds of people see "sold out" for those seats. With no expiry, those seats stay locked for the whole sale. A hold with an expiry exists for exactly this reason. Its price: a held seat is out of everyone else's reach for up to 10 minutes, so also cap how many active holds one user may have (say 4).

items.meaning: Keeping a thing reserved for someone for a while, until it is confirmed or the time runs out.
The record of the whole claim, covering the hold and the later confirmation.

check.q: Why do you need a hold with an expiry while the payment is in progress? What goes wrong with only holding, or only booking after payment?
check.a: Booking after payment can leave someone who has paid without a seat. Holding with no expiry lets users who walked away block the seat forever. An expiry fixes both.

slides.title: The life of a hold: four states
slides.tldr: Every hold is a record: from held it becomes either confirmed, or expired or canceled. The expiry lives in the record's expires_at column.

blocks.body: Rather than writing "held" on the seat itself, create a separate **reservation record**. It holds which seat, for whom, what state it is in, and `expires_at`. The state changes along three paths: confirmed when payment arrives, expired when time runs out, canceled when the user lets go. For product stock the idea is the same, except you count `reserved` instead of seats.

blocks.caption: The four states of a reservation record and the paths between them

nodes.label: held
nodes.tip: The hold has been created. Until expires_at, the seat belongs to this user.

nodes.label: confirmed
nodes.tip: Payment has arrived. This is a final state; it never changes again.

nodes.label: expired
nodes.tip: The time is up and the seat is free again. Also a final state.

nodes.label: canceled
nodes.tip: The user canceled it. The seat is free at once.

edges.label: payment succeeds
edges.tip: Only if payment arrives before the expiry.

blocks.body: A hold is a claim with an expiry. The truth about the expiry lives in expires_at.

aside.body: From held you can go three ways; from confirmed, expired or canceled there is no way back.

check.q: Which three events take a `held` record to a final state?
check.a: Successful payment gives confirmed, passing expires_at gives expired, and the user letting go gives canceled. There is no way back from any of these three final states.

slides.title: Building a hold: a unique index and an expiring row
slides.tldr: Put a partial unique index on active holds; expire stale ones before creating a new hold; if the unique rule fires, the seat is taken.

blocks.body: Checking first and then inserting is not enough. At 10:00:00 Ryan and Kevin both ask for seat 12: both SELECTs say "free", both INSERTs run, and the seat has two holds. The index below makes the database itself refuse the second insert.

marks.tip: This one index is what prevents double-booking. If two requests insert at the same time, only one survives.
The expiry time is stored on the row itself, so you can always tell how long a hold lasts.
Take the time from ClockInterface. That way a test can move time forward by hand.
Even after a hold has run out, its row still says 'held'. The unique index treats that as active, so you must expire it first.
If someone else already got a hold, the exception arrives here, meaning this seat is no longer free.

items: For product stock, use a `reserved` column instead of per-seat rows: `UPDATE product SET reserved = reserved + :n WHERE id = :id AND stock - reserved >= :n`.
For stock, still keep a separate reservation row for each hold request, or at expiry you can't tell how much to give back.
MySQL has no partial indexes. Workaround: a nullable `active_seat_id` column equal to the seat id while the hold is active, NULL after expiry or cancel, with a UNIQUE index on it.

check.q: When two users ask to hold the same seat at the same moment, who wins, and what does the other get?
check.a: The partial unique index lets through whichever insert arrives first. The other gets a UniqueConstraintViolationException, which is shown as a SeatTaken error.

slides.title: Confirm and clean up: expiry is the truth, cleanup is just sweeping
slides.tldr: When confirming, verify that expires_at is still in the future; the cleanup job only keeps things tidy, and correctness doesn't depend on it.

marks.tip: The old state (held) and the expiry still being in the future are in one condition. This is compare-and-swap.
0 means the hold no longer exists: it expired or was canceled. Either way, it cannot be confirmed.
Runs every minute. To run it you need a `php bin/console messenger:consume scheduler_default` worker.
Just sweeping: it keeps reports and dashboards tidy. Confirm and new holds do not depend on it.

blocks.body: Expiry is checked at the moment of use. The cleanup job is only a broom.

aside.body: Even if the cleanup job is down, late, or runs twice, hold correctness is intact, because confirm and a new hold each check the expiry themselves.

check.q: The cleanup job was down for an hour. Can an expired hold still be confirmed in that time? Why?
check.a: No. The confirm UPDATE has the condition `expires_at > now`, so after the expiry it changes 0 rows and raises HoldExpired. Correctness holds even when cleanup doesn't run.

slides.title: Payment arrives after the expiry: now what?
slides.tldr: When payment is slow, the money can arrive after the hold ran out; if the seat has gone to someone else, that payment must be refunded, never quietly confirmed.

blocks.body: Ryan starts paying in the last moment of his 10 minutes, the gateway is slow, and the success notice arrives **after** the expiry. By then Kevin has already held the seat. Ryan's money has been taken, but the seat is no longer his. You have to accept that this will happen, and plan for it.

blocks.caption: The payment lands after the expiry, and Kevin gets Ryan's seat

actors.label: Ryan
actors.tip: Held seat 12 and went off to pay.

actors.label: Kevin
actors.tip: Asked for seat 12 after Ryan's hold ran out.

actors.label: Booking system
actors.tip: Handles holds and confirmations.

messages.label: Hold seat 12, 10:00
messages.tip: The hold lasts until 10:10.

messages.label: Hold seat 12, 10:11
messages.tip: Ryan's hold has expired, so Kevin gets it.

messages.label: Payment succeeds, 10:12
messages.tip: The gateway reported it late.
The WHERE needs status = held and expires_at > now; Ryan's hold is expired, so it doesn't match.

messages.label: Money back, no seat
messages.tip: Send a refund request to the gateway and tell the user clearly.

blocks.title: When a late payment arrives
items: Confirm with the same CAS as before; a 0 means the seat is gone.
If the seat is gone, send an automatic refund through the gateway.
Tell the user what happened, and let them pick a new seat.

marks.tip: confirm() threw HoldExpired, meaning 0 rows changed: the seat is no longer Ryan's.
The key is built from the payment id, so if this message is delivered twice the gateway refunds once.

items: A refund is not free: some gateways keep their fee, and the money takes days to reach the customer. One more reason to keep late payments rare.
Whether it is valid to confirm a late payment when the seat is still free is a business decision. Even then, do it with a CAS, not just by looking at `status`.
If the hold's expiry is shorter than the payment time, this will happen every day. Set the expiry longer than the gateway's maximum time.

check.q: Ryan's payment succeeded, but the seat has gone to someone else. What is the correct system behavior?
check.a: The confirm fails (0 rows), and the system sends a refund through the gateway, tells Ryan clearly, and lets him pick another seat. It must never quietly give two people the same seat.

slides.title: Saved in the database, but nobody was told
slides.tldr: When you write to the database and then to another system (a queue, email, another service), a failure in between leaves one done and the other not. This is the dual-write problem.

blocks.title: Writing in the ledger, then phoning the courier
blocks.body: A shopkeeper writes an order in his ledger, then phones the courier to come and collect the goods. He writes the order but forgets to call, or the phone line drops. The customer has an order, but the goods will never ship. Writes to two separate places never happen together.

marks.tip: COMMIT happens here. After this, the order stays in the database whatever happens.
If this line never runs, the order exists but the warehouse and the email service know nothing. Write in the opposite order and you get phantom notifications instead.

blocks.caption: A failure between the two steps: the order is saved, the notification is lost

actors.label: Symfony app
actors.tip: Writes to two places one after the other: the database first, then the queue.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Committed the order correctly.

actors.label: Message broker
actors.tip: Delivers news to the warehouse, email and other services. Here the news never arrived.

messages.tip: If the app stops at exactly this moment, the second write never happens. And nobody sees any error.

messages.note: Warehouse never learns of the order
messages.tip: The customer has paid and the goods won't ship. It surfaces days later as a complaint.

blocks.body: Two ways out. Make both systems commit together (two-phase commit, next slide), which is rarely worth the trouble. Or write the message into the same database transaction as the order (the outbox, the slide after that).

items.meaning: Writing one event to two separate systems (a database and a queue) one after the other, with no way to commit both together.
One "all or nothing" job that spans several separate systems.

aside.title: The lost-order complaints
aside.body: An e-commerce site got 10 to 15 complaints a month of "payment made but goods never arrived". It turned out that at deploy time, some orders had reached the database but the notification never got to the queue.

check.q: The code commits to the database and then dispatches to a queue. If the process dies before the dispatch, what happens?
check.a: The order stays in the database, but the OrderPlaced message is never sent. The warehouse and email service never find out, and nobody sees an error.

slides.title: Two-phase commit: getting everyone's "yes", and why it is avoided
slides.tldr: In 2PC, a coordinator first asks everyone "ready?" and commits only if all say yes; but if the coordinator dies, everyone is left stuck.

blocks.title: The officiant asking for consent
blocks.body: At a wedding, the officiant first asks both partners, "Do you accept?" Only if both say yes is the marriage sealed; if either says no, nothing happens. That is 2PC: phase one is prepare (getting consent), phase two is commit (the announcement). If the officiant faints after the consent but before the announcement, both sides are stuck, not knowing whether it happened.

blocks.caption: Two-phase commit: everyone agrees first, then everyone commits together

actors.label: Officiant (coordinator)
actors.tip: Coordinates the whole job; the decision rests with it alone.

actors.label: Database A
actors.tip: The orders database.

actors.label: Database B
actors.tip: The inventory database.

messages.label: PREPARE: ready?
messages.tip: Phase 1: A gets its work ready, holds its locks, and promises it can commit.

messages.label: Yes, I accept
messages.tip: This "yes" can't be taken back. Now B can only wait for the coordinator.

messages.label: COMMIT
messages.tip: Phase 2: everyone said yes, so it is final now.

blocks.title: Why it is usually avoided
items: If the coordinator or the network fails midway, A and B sit holding locks (blocking).
Every phase costs a network round trip, so it is slow, and locks are held longer.
Email, SMS and external HTTP APIs don't understand 2PC. Not every system supports XA.

blocks.body: When outside systems are involved, skip 2PC: use an outbox, sagas and idempotency.

use: Two XA-capable databases in the same company, low traffic, an experienced team
avoid: Outside APIs, queues, email or many services involved
High traffic or a need for fast responses

items.meaning: The common standard for 2PC between databases and a transaction manager.

check.q: After every participant has said "yes" to PREPARE, the coordinator dies. What happens?
check.a: The participants don't know whether to commit or roll back, so they sit holding their locks. Until the coordinator returns, nobody else can work on those rows.

slides.title: Outbox: write the notification in the same transaction
slides.tldr: Write the notification into an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a separate relay sends it to the queue later. The notification can't get lost.

blocks.body: The fix: don't write to two places, write to the same database. The order and the note "this message must be sent" go into one transaction, so they commit together or are canceled together. Then a separate relay reads the outbox, sends the messages to the broker, and marks them as sent. Think of a mail carrier's delivery list.

marks.tip: The outbox row is in the same database as orders. On COMMIT both stay; on ROLLBACK both go.
SKIP LOCKED: when several relays run, two of them never pick up the same row.
If the dispatch succeeds but the UPDATE or COMMIT afterwards fails, the message goes out again. That is at-least-once, so the consumer needs idempotency.

items: An outbox never gives exactly-once. It won't lose a message, but it may send one twice. That is why the idempotent consumer on the next slide is essential.
Add a job to delete old published rows, or the outbox table keeps growing.
The price is delay. With a 5-second relay the warehouse can hear up to 5 seconds late. Fine for orders and emails, wrong for anything that must react at once.
Skip the outbox when one database holds everything, or when losing a message is harmless (say, a "page viewed" counter).
In a small app, if Messenger's Doctrine transport uses the same connection, the dispatch itself becomes part of that transaction; that is how you get a simple outbox.

check.q: Why does putting the notification in an outbox close the gap between the order's COMMIT and a lost message?
check.a: The order and the message are written in one transaction, so both commit or both are canceled. The relay sends from the outbox later, so a pending message is never lost.

slides.title: Saga: every step has an "undo step"
slides.tldr: Break a job spanning many services into small steps; if a step fails, undo the earlier successful steps in reverse order with compensations.

blocks.body: An online order involves four services: order, payment, stock and courier. They are all separate, so a single rollback across them is impossible. So each service finishes its own transaction and tells the next step. If something gets stuck, the earlier steps run their own **compensation**, such as refunding the money. Instead of a database rollback, it is an "undoing action that makes amends". Who notices the failure and starts the undoing, and what if an undo fails too? The next slide shows it.

blocks.caption: A four-step saga, and the undo step for each
headers: Undo, if a later step fails

rows.tip: The first step succeeded. If any later step fails, the order is marked canceled.
The charge is already committed in another database. It can't be erased, so you need an opposite refund transaction.
If the courier step fails, the stock must be freed again.

cells: Requests a pickup from the courier
rows.tip: The last step. If this one fails it has nothing of its own to undo, so the saga undoes the earlier three in reverse order (3, 2, 1).

blocks.body: A saga has no rollback; it has an undo action for each step.

aside.body: When it fails, undo the earlier steps in reverse order: 3, 2, 1.

items.meaning: One coordinator runs the steps in order.
Each service listens for events and does its next job itself, with no coordinator in the middle.

check.q: The courier booking failed. Which steps does the saga undo, and in what order?
check.a: In reverse order: first it releases the stock hold (3), then refunds the payment (2), and finally marks the order canceled (1).

slides.title: Starting the undo steps, and what if an undo fails
slides.tldr: An orchestrator records each finished step; on a failure it undoes them last to first, one message at a time. A failed undo is retried until it works, so every undo must be safe to repeat.

blocks.body: Someone has to notice the failure and start the undoing. Here a small orchestrator runs the steps and writes each finished one into a `saga` table. When a step fails, it flips the saga to "compensating" and sends one `CompensateNext` message. The handler undoes the latest finished step, then sends the next message, so the order stays 3, 2, 1. If an undo throws (the payment provider is down), Messenger retries it, and nothing else moves until it works.

marks.tip: Saved before anything is undone. If the app dies now, a restart sees "compensating" and carries on undoing.
Starts the undo chain: one message, which undoes only the latest finished step.
It can run twice (a crash right after it, before removeDone). So the refund must use the saga id as its idempotency key and pay at most once.
A step is struck off only after its undo succeeded, so a failure never skips a step.

blocks.body: An undo can fail too: retry it until it works, and make it safe to repeat.

items: Set `retry_strategy` (for example max_retries 5, multiplier 3: waits of 1, 3, 9, 27, 81 seconds) and a `failure_transport`, and alert a person when a message lands there. A stuck refund must never go unseen.
An undo is not a perfect rewind: a sent email can't be unsent, so you send a correction. And while the saga runs, others can see half-done state (order pending, stock held).

use: One business job spanning several services, each with its own database
avoid: A single database can wrap it all in one transaction: use that, it is simpler

check.q: The refund undo throws because the payment provider is down. What happens to the saga?
check.a: The CompensateNext message is retried with growing waits and the saga stays "compensating", so no later undo runs. If the retries run out, it lands in the failure transport and a person is alerted.

slides.title: Arrives twice, runs once: the idempotent consumer
slides.tldr: An outbox, retries and the broker can all deliver the same message more than once. A consumer that remembers each message id and does nothing the second time is safe.

blocks.body: Because of the outbox and retries, a message arrives **at least once**, and sometimes twice. An ordinary handler then awards points twice or sends the email twice. The fix: every message has an id, and the handler first inserts that id into a table. If the insert doesn't go through (it's already there), the work was done earlier, and the handler quietly returns.

marks.tip: There is no duplicate check. A broker retry or a second send by the relay turns straight into extra money or points.
processed_message has a unique constraint on the (message_id, handler) pair. Even if two workers arrive together, only one gets in.
0 means this id was already inserted. Because awarding the points is in the same transaction, the work and the "done" marker commit together.

items: Putting outside work like email inside the transaction makes duplicates hard to stop. Where possible, use the provider's idempotency key.
Create the message id once per event (the outbox row's id), not on every send.

check.q: If the same OrderPlaced event arrives twice, how does the handler award the points only once?
check.a: The first time, it manages to insert the message_id, so it awards the points. The second time, ON CONFLICT gives affected rows 0, so it returns without doing anything.
